analysis.one_liner: Transfers the United States Postal Service to a private corporation, with shares going first to postal employees.
analysis.headline: The bill to privatize the Postal Service never left a House subcommittee, dying there without a hearing or a vote in the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would hand all property of the U.S. Postal Service to a private corporation set up by nine incorporators elected by postal employees — and it explicitly requires that no payment be made for any of those assets. Employees would receive stock in the new company for the first year, after which shares could be sold to the general public. The new company would deliver mail under the same universal-service and rate principles for at least five years, after which Congress would be asked to repeal or rewrite the federal laws governing mail service.
analysis.who_benefits: The new private corporation, which would acquire the entire Postal Service — its buildings, fleet, network, and legal rights — at no cost. Postal employees would gain first-year ownership shares and a guarantee of comparable retirement benefits. After one year, investors buying the shares on the open market would gain ownership of the former public mail system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The new corporation, its employee-shareholders, then public investors

how_it_helps.text: Postal employees would receive securities in the new corporation allocated by years of service and level of compensation, and retirement benefits would have to match what they would have earned under the Postal Service.

The corporation would be required to provide postal service consistent with the universal-service and rate principles in existing federal law during its first years, and the mail monopoly (the private express statutes) would stay in place for five years.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would give away a nationwide public asset — the entire postal network — without any payment in return, and postal customers, whose mail service would pass from a publicly accountable agency to a private company whose long-term rates and service obligations would depend on future legislation Congress had yet to write.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires that no payment be made for any rights or assets of the Postal Service transferred to the corporation, so a nationwide public asset built by taxpayers would change hands for free.

After the first year, shares could be sold to the general public 'under such terms and conditions as the corporation considers appropriate,' meaning control of the mail system could end up with whoever buys the stock, and rate-setting during the transition would rest on presidential recommendations rather than settled law.

The private express statutes protecting universal mail delivery would continue for only five years, after which the President would recommend repealing or modifying federal statutes, leaving the future of universal service obligations to later legislation that did not yet exist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The employee-ownership feature is real — workers would get shares and a retirement guarantee — but the core of the bill is a no-charge transfer of an entire public agency's assets to a private corporation, with public accountability over rates and universal service dependent on future recommendations and legislation. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the public would be giving away, for nothing, an asset it spent more than two centuries building, in exchange for promises about service that would largely expire after five years.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee and then to its Postal Service Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Government Reform and Oversight, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Postal Service on January 15, 1995.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill died in subcommittee when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Postal customers and postal employees who wanted the service kept public came out ahead: the mail system stayed a public agency, and the corporations and investors who would have acquired its assets for free gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Postal customers; the service stayed public

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 104th Congress and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: House Committee on Government Reform and Oversight
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Postal Service Subcommittee and never reported it back for a floor vote.

against.name: Postal unions
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed privatizing the Postal Service, which would have ended it as a public employer.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and the bill died quietly in a Republican-controlled committee without any floor vote.

industries.industry: Private mail and package delivery companies
industries.note: A privatized Postal Service would set the stage for the private express statutes — the rules that bar private carriers from ordinary letter mail — to be repealed or modified after five years, opening the letter market. The bill's structure would hand the incumbent network to private owners rather than keep a public alternative in place.

Employees would get ownership shares based on seniority and pay, plus a retirement guarantee, but their employer would shift from a public agency with civil-service protections to a corporation that could be sold to outside investors after a year.

After the initial one-year employee period, shares in the new corporation could be offered to the general public on terms the corporation itself chose, creating a new tradable asset carved out of a public agency.
